clue.text: Hard on the heels of swinging single people

indicators.note: to be on someone's heels is to follow right behind, so one piece comes straight after another
something swinging moves to and fro, so its letters are set loose and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A tough type tailing swingers at a singles night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard' leads the clue but its letter goes last, because it follows the rearranged word. The definition is the single word at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The English are a nation, so the word works as a collective noun for a whole national group of inhabitants.

clue.text: see 25 dn.
Shy about hair balls

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the word is written backwards

parts.note: to shy is to throw, as is to lob
locks are tresses of hair

explanation.surface: Someone bashful about body hair, or a coy remark about hairy testicles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shy' looks like the adjective for timid, but it is the verb meaning to throw, as at a coconut shy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for testicles, and both are also used as an exclamation meaning nonsense.

clue.text: Un-PC wife: "Not both testicles with coupling"

parts.note: one testicle rather than the pair
with and 'and' both mean together with
a chain is a linking or coupling device

explanation.surface: A politically incorrect wife complaining about her husband's anatomy and their sex life.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted remark looks like the wife speaking, but it is the wordplay; 'Un-PC wife' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an old, sexist joke term for a wife, picturing marriage as a prisoner's shackle and weight.

clue.text: Love gets one into 'talc' variation of shagging

indicators.note: going into something puts it inside, so one piece sits within the other
a variation is a changed version, so these letters appear in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: to get something is to acquire it, so one piece is joined straight onto another

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, shaped like O
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Talcum powder as a novel addition to lovemaking.
explanation.walkthrough: The talc letters are reordered as C and TAL, and the love-plus-one pair goes between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Coitus is sexual intercourse, so the adjective describes anything relating to the act, which is the slang shagging.

clue.text: Tory leader unclear about extremes of Conference's aversion

indicators.note: moved about means shifted around, so the letters are jumbled
a leader is at the front, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of the word
taken as written, then rearranged with the letter before it

indicators.note: the extremes are the two far ends, so only the first and last letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A Conservative leader dithering over the party conference, which they would rather avoid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unclear' reads as describing the leader's position, but it is letters to be mixed with the leader's initial; the 's links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Reluctance is unwillingness or disinclination to do something, close in meaning to a dislike or distaste.

clue.text: Prick takes on the French hacks accommodated here

indicators.note: to take something on is to add it to yourself, so one piece is followed by another

parts.note: to prick is to stab, as with a needle
les is French for the, in the plural

explanation.surface: A nasty journalist taking on French reporters, in the Private Eye habit of calling journalists hacks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hacks' points at journalists, but here they are hired or riding horses, also called hacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Stables are buildings where horses are housed, and a hack is an ordinary riding horse.

clue.text: (& 24ac./16ac.) Successful lobby group that calls the shots?

definitions.text: Successful lobby group that calls the shots?

parts.note: surface reading: a powerful pressure group that is in control and decides policy

parts.words: lobby group that calls the shots
parts.note: setter's reading: a gun lobby, whose business is literally firing shots

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'calls the shots' means to be in charge; read literally it suggests guns. This is the powerful American gun-rights lobby, known as the NRA.
explanation.definitionFit: The organisation is a famously influential US pressure group campaigning for firearm ownership, so it both controls politicians and concerns shooting.

clue.text: see 11ac.
Clumsy hulk separating local Labour leaders — might be button-holed

indicators.note: to separate two things is to come between them, so one piece is placed in the middle
leaders go at the front, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: first letters of each word
a big, clumsy oaf can be called an ape

explanation.surface: A lumbering bruiser coming between two Labour figures, who might be buttonholed by him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'button-holed' sounds like being cornered for a chat, but a lapel literally has a buttonhole cut into it.
explanation.definitionFit: The folded front flap of a jacket usually carries a small slit for a flower or badge, so it is literally holed.

clue.text: (& 9ac.) Watts used to get this sudden inspiration?

parts.note: setter's reading: wattage is the power rating of the household lamp that switches on
surface reading: an instant when an idea suddenly occurs to someone

explanation.surface: Someone called Watts who used to have brainwaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watts' looks like a person's surname, but it is the unit of power printed on domestic lamps; cartoons show a lamp above a head for an idea.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an informal idiom for a flash of understanding, from the cartoon image of an illuminated glass globe.

clue.text: Develop big hips when diets do this?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: literally take on the figure of the fruit, wide at the bottom

definitions.note: the clue supplies a situation; the answer is the phrase meaning what diets do
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the British idiom for going wrong or failing

explanation.surface: Putting on weight around the hips, which is what happens when diets fail.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that a failed diet does both at once: it goes wrong, and you literally gain a bottom-heavy figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is British slang for a plan failing badly, and literally describes a body widening below the waist.

clue.text: One element of stupid-sounding little politician

indicators.note: sounding means as heard, so the word is spelt by how it is pronounced

parts.note: silly means stupid; the spelling follows the sound
Con is the short form of Conservative

explanation.surface: A sneer at a small-time politician with a stupid manner of speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little' here means abbreviated, so the politician is shortened to the party label used on British ballots.
explanation.definitionFit: Silicon is a chemical element, number 14 in the periodic table, so it is one member of that set.

clue.text: Editorial's cool … on what Theresa May's failed to show?

definitions.text: what Theresa May's failed to show

indicators.note: in a down answer one thing sitting on another is directly above it, so the pieces follow in order

parts.note: a leader is a newspaper editorial; the 's supplies the final S
hip means fashionably cool

explanation.surface: A newspaper editorial coolly commenting on Theresa May's failings as Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a leader or leading article is a newspaper's editorial. Theresa May was the UK Prime Minister widely criticised as weak and indecisive.
explanation.definitionFit: Leadership is the quality of guiding and commanding others, which critics said the Prime Minister lacked.

clue.text: Board showing constraint, acquired by Crown

indicators.note: what is acquired is taken in and held, so one piece ends up inside the other

parts.note: the pate is the crown or top of the head
a let is an obstruction, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: A company board under restrictions after being bought by the Crown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crown' looks like the monarchy, but it means the top of the head. 'Board' looks like company directors; it is a flat piece of wood.
explanation.definitionFit: A palette is the thin wooden board a painter holds to mix colours on.

clue.text: see 8ac.
Unfading Democrat ultimately in wrong

indicators.note: being in something means placed inside it, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: immoral means morally wrong

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A US Democrat who never fades away despite being in the wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' is the adjective for ethically bad, not an error, which is what opens the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something immortal never dies or perishes, so its fame or life does not fade away.

clue.text: Bush, lip trembling, is to fulfil a writer's dream?

indicators.note: trembling is shaking, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: President Bush, lip quivering, about to realise an author's ambition, perhaps with his memoirs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' reads as the former US president, but both words simply provide letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Every aspiring author hopes to see their book printed and issued, so getting it into print fulfils that ambition.

clue.text: Character of German city Conservative — gutless

indicators.note: with its guts removed, a word loses all its inside letters

parts.note: Essen is a city in the Ruhr, Germany
the word with every middle letter removed

explanation.surface: A spineless German politician from a city's conservative party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutless' sounds like cowardice, but it removes the inside of the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The essence of something is its fundamental nature or intrinsic quality, which is what its character means.

clue.text: Piss-taker — in future, thrash!

indicators.note: the letters sit in the following words, running straight across the gap between them

parts.note: read across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Someone threatening to beat a mocker, or a 'piss-taker', in future.
explanation.walkthrough: A piss-taker is British slang for someone who mocks; read literally it is the body's tube that takes urine out.
explanation.definitionFit: The urethra is the duct carrying urine from the bladder, so it literally takes the piss away.

clue.text: Passionate shag that might add inches to your melons?

definitions.text: that might add inches to your melons?

parts.note: hot means passionate or ardent
to bed someone is to have sex with them

explanation.surface: A steamy sex session supposedly good for breast enlargement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'melons' is slang for breasts in the surface, but here they are the fruit grown in a garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Gardeners use a heated bed of soil or manure to force plants such as melons to grow bigger.

clue.text: Two males taking drug when lancing gentlemen's boils

indicators.note: a lance pierces into something, so this piece is pushed inside the other

parts.note: sirs is a polite term for gentlemen

indicators.note: taking something means adding it to yourself, so one piece joins the next

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for male, twice
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Two men on drugs lancing a gentleman's boils, a grim medical scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boils' looks like the plural noun for skin abscesses, but it is the verb, and the 's is the plural of gentlemen.
explanation.definitionFit: To simmer is to cook gently just below or at bubbling point, a near synonym of heating to bubble.

clue.text: US-Italian arrangement that went down controversially

indicators.note: an arrangement sets things in a chosen order, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A US-Italian diplomatic deal that was badly received.
explanation.walkthrough: 'went down' sounds like how a deal was received; it really means sank.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocean liner was torpedoed by a German submarine in 1915, and the sinking of a ship carrying passengers and munitions was hugely contentious.

clue.text: see 8ac.
(& 2dn.) Dot's loaded, upsetting corporations

parts.note: loaded means filled up

indicators.note: to upset is to knock over, and in a down answer that turns the word upside down

parts.note: a corporation is old slang for a big belly, as is a pot

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dot' looks like a woman's name and 'loaded' like being rich; 'corporations' are not businesses but paunches.

clue.text: The Sun: evidence of a beating?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: something that shines brightly in the sky
second meaning: slang for a black eye

explanation.walkthrough: The Sun looks like the British tabloid newspaper, which suggests exposing a scandal, but here it is the star that shines.
explanation.definitionFit: A bright light source is literally a thing that gives light, and slang uses the same word for a bruised, blackened eye.

clue.text: Iron-like Margaret's opener: "Tell CIA to get lost"

indicators.note: an opener comes first, so only the initial letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of the name

indicators.note: something lost goes astray, so the letters wander into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Margaret Thatcher, the Iron Lady, opening a speech by telling the CIA to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Thatcher was nicknamed the Iron Lady, so 'Iron-like Margaret' looks like one phrase; the definition is only the first word.
